utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning and may I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm Thomas Hannis along with Crispian Smith on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should indicate that Mr. Dobbyn is also a part of the Prosecution team this morning. I didn't see him behind me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the witness returned to the stand please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I would remind you that you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Panic. The first thing I'd like to show you is 65 ter number 340. And this is a document that doesn't have a date on it, but it appears to be the quarterly report for the Zvornik Police Station for the months of July, August, and September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go quickly to the last page at the bottom so the witness could have a look at the name and the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You recognise who's signed this document, Mr. Panic?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Milorad Lokancevic, chief of police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this document. I have no questions about it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What is the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a quarterly report for the Zvornik police station for three months during July, August, and September. It's a contemporaneous document, and it contains information that corroborates some of his earlier testimony and links up with other documents that we have submitted and will submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: When you say it corroborates information, could you on a thumbnail indicate what that corroboration is?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, regarding the police securing certain facilities in town including the Zvornik prison, regarding their activities and combat activities, regarding the fact that a number of police officers from the reserve force had been removed, regarding the number of documents that have been sent and received to show communications. We think it's relevant and probative and would ask you to accept it at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P347, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Next I would like to show the witness 65 ter number 1793.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, this is a -- this is a package of documents or reports regarding Zvornik Police Station for 1992, and this is the -- the collection of documents that we gave you yesterday as a hard copy for you to review after the second break. Did you have a chance to look at that document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Not entirely, I just glanced at it. And I apologise, this is not only the report of the police station, it refers to the report of the whole security centre, which is superior to all the others and also includes a plan programme work for 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the chief of station who signed those documents was Mr. Lokancevic?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the public security station, whereas the police station is a different matter. This is the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you explain the difference for us between the public security station and what I heard translated as the police station?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public security station is a higher level. And within its organisation structure it has a police station, CID, administrative and legal department, communications department, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. And the -- the state security is also a part of that higher organisation?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The state security is a separate organisational unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And under whose supervision would the local state security head be? Does he have to respond to Mr. Lokancevic, or does he respond to somebody in Bijeljina? How did that work, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wouldn't answer to Lokancevic. As I said, it's a separate unit, and I think that the state security was directly answerable to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to turn to page 20 of the English and page 17 of the B/C/S in e-court, if we may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, I don't know if you had a chance -- sorry. Mr. Panic, I don't know if you had a chance to see this portion when you reviewed it yesterday. But this is the section describing the measures and activities aimed at creating and functioning of the Republika Srpska MUP. And if you could look at the first full paragraph after item A. And I'm reading from my English translation. It says: "As is well known, the Zvornik SJB had operated within the Tuzla CSB until 4 April 1992." And then it goes on to say: "As of early January 1992, a group of six SJB employees was in permanent contact with the steering committee of the SDS. The aim was to prepare the detaching of the SJB in the event of municipal territory being divided into Serb and Muslim part." Were you one of those six?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't among the six employees mentioned here, but on one occasion, I don't know the exact date, I was summoned to come to Mali Zvornik to attend a meeting where I got a negative appraisal because I had been a member of the League of Communists in the past, but I did go and attend this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go next to page 18 in the B/C/S and page 21 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And about two-thirds of the way down, Mr. Panic, you'll see an item B. It says: "On 4 April, 1992, the chief and the assistant chief of the SJB went to a meeting of the Crisis Staff in Ugljevik in order to make arrangements for further activities." On 4th of April, 1992, who would that have been, the chief and the assistant chief by name?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Vasilic was the commander -- or, rather, Dragan Spasojevic had already been appointed, whereas Vasilic was the assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if -- yeah, we could go to the bottom of the page in B/C/S and to the top of page 22 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The last paragraph is translated as: "After that incident, the assistant chief and the assistant in charge of reserve forces went to a meeting in Mali Zvornik at which a decision was made to extract the vehicles, equipment, materiel, and technical equipment and to put up barricades in Karakaj." Is this a meeting you just spoke about a minute ago that you said you attended?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is it correct that you were the assist in charge of the reserve forces at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assistant for the reserve forces at the Zvornik station. However, there were numerous reserve forces and assistants and commanders. I'm not sure about this extraction of vehicles. The only possibility is that Slavko Eric and Marinko were there, whereas I was at a different meeting where this topic was not being discussed, and there were several numbers -- members of the SDS, Dragan the commander and Milan Micic. Milan Micic and I were given this minus mark because we were not members of the SDS but, rather, members of the former League of Communists. I'm not sure about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If would could next turning to page 20 of the B/C/S and page 24 of the English. Top of the page in English, and near the bottom in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, I want to direct your attention to what's item number 1, about a fourth of the way up from the bottom. Here in the report it says: "Until -- to 4 April 1992, six senior employees, Dragan Spasojevic, Marinko Vasilic, Slavko Eric, Petko Panic, Milan Milic, and Miko Miljanovic worked on the organisation and detachment of the Serb SJB from the original SJB which existed up to that point." So again it looks like the chief who is writing this report has you as one of the original six. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a certain extent it is correct, but this chief was not there at the time, but after his arrival he had probably been informed. If there had been any assignment, the Serbian Zvornik police station was already established. Spasojevic was the commander. His deputy was Marinko Vasilic. He gave us certain tasks to perform relating to surveillance, because sometime on the 23rd or the 24th the commander deputy Dragan Karovic [as interpreted] mobilised only Muslim police employees, surrounded the SUP building, and the next day we had a meeting where the inspector from the Tuzla CSB came and negotiations were started how to proceed with the work in the future. I think, then, after that on the 3rd or the 4th in Sapna, the Muslims killed the warrant officer second class and wounded another soldier, which grew into an incident of larger proportions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Page 7, line 9. I believe the name of the commander deputy was not recorded properly, because the witness said something different. If you can check with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Panic? Could you repeat the name of the Muslim deputy commander who mobilised Muslim employees?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was deputy commander for traffic. Adnan Karovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to page 21 of the B/C/S and remain on 24 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, you see a section entitled "Participation of MUP members in combat operations." And item D, the fourth one down on my list says: "About 20 policemen took part in the securing and guarding of collective centres." And as of the writing of this report, the end of December 1992, it says: "At present, 11 policemen are guarding just one such centre." I believe that's consistent with what you told us yesterday in your testimony, that the police were taking part in guarding those collection centres that were set up for all the Muslims who were being detained by the various formations operating in Zvornik earlier in 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This probably refers to the Novi Izvor prison and the misdemeanour court which remained there throughout the 1992 and all the way through the early 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And continuing on down that page another three or four items down, one says: "One active police employee was on loan to the VRS along with 150 reserve policemen." Again, can you inform us how that worked. How were MUP employees loaned to the army, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that yesterday I said that already at that time there was no need for such a large number of policemen who were actually reserve police officers due to certain weaknesses. The chief, therefore, decided probably at the brigade commander's request who said that he needed new -- extra men to downsize the number of the police officer -- officers so that 150 of them were seconded to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And immediately below that it says: "Due to various other reasons which render them unfit for work in the OUP, ten reserve policemen were on loan to the VRS." Do you know anything about why these ten reserve policemen were not fit for work in the OUP? And can you tell us what OUP stands for.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That stands for internal affairs organ, OUP. Well, probably this was due to some conduct that didn't become policemen. I just suppose that was the reason. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could next turn to page 43 of the English and page 36 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, about a third of the way up from the bottom you'll see one line that says: "Five vehicles were seized during operation TAS," T-A-S. Do you know what that referred to?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On leaving Sarajevo, certain individuals from the TAS company used to take away Golf vehicles with them. During the searches and inspection, these vehicles were detected and subsequently impounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Page 40 of the B/C/S, please. That would be page 46 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We have a list of manpower, and about two-thirds of the way down there's a paragraph that contains the number 115. My English says: "Due to errors made in service and the fact that they had violated the moral norms of our people, 150 [sic] reserve policemen had been stripped from the RR and have been placed at the disposal of the Serb army." First of all, can you explain to us what RR stands for in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The suggested translation in my English is "wartime assignment."

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, wartime assignment. Yes, yes. Instead of being deployed in the police, they were deployed in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was any other action taken against them for whatever violations of the moral norms that they had committed other than simply kicking them out of the police and turning them over to the army? Do you know were there were any disciplinary proceedings or any criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had not committed any criminal offences, no criminal proceedings were instituted. As for disciplinary proceedings, since most of them were reserve policemen no action was taken against them. The punishment meted out to them was that they were deployed in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The last page I'd like to look at in this document is page 50 of the B/C/S, page 56 of the English. Do you recognise the name and the signature at the bottom of this page?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise it. Vukasin Danojlovic, chief of communication sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that his job in 1992 in the Zvornik SJB?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before the war and during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In his report we see the number of Official Notes sent as 590 -- or 391, and those received 590. And he indicates that operations of the shortwave radio and the telephone exchange were carried out around the clock. I know you told us early in the first ten days or so of the conflict that there were some problems with communications. But this seems to indicate that after that, they were working adequately. Is that consistent with your experience?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the first days, the communications system did not function, especially not amongst us, the police forces, because we did not have enough equipment or anything. And up there when communications were established, well -- well, five, six, ten days upon the entry of Arkan's people, I mean everything was destroyed, and then it was repaired later, and that depends -- so it depends on when the communications were restored.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And this gentleman would be in a better position to know about that than you because it was his job; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was chief of communications. He is the only one who could know that. For instance, no one could enter the premises of the communications department, and he was commander and they were working there doing their job, using teleprinters and whatever else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender 1793.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have an objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I speak in Serbian just to be very clear about it. [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document contains several different documents within it, and it is difficult to establish what this is exactly about. Namely, Mr. Hannis showed one report during the first part. Actually, in this document, on page 1, it says that the document consists of the methodology for compiling reports, then the report of the SJB Zvornik for 1992 along with the appropriate text, and the programme of the SJB work for 1993. That's what it says on page 1. In the document itself there are two reports for 1992. One is the one that Mr. Hannis dealt with during his first few questions, whereas the latter part of his questions were from the second report. One is dated December 1992, and the other report is dated January 1993. That document that Mr. Hannis used in the first part between pages 5 and 6, obviously a different typewriter was used, ERN number 01769088 and ERN number 01769089. These two reports absolutely do differ, considerably so. I admit that both were signed by Lokancevic on the last page. However, it is obvious that for some reason, either two reports were written up or one of the two reports is not the right report. On pages 01769081, that's the ERN number, that is the document that is attached to the report dated December 1992, and the second one, again an accompanying document. The ERN number is 01769082. That pertains to the one from 1993. I think that in this way in which Mr. Hannis chose to proceed when putting his questions to the witness in respect of certain facts from this report, this simply isn't good enough to have this admitted into evidence. There is a strong suspicion regarding the authenticity of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may. Your Honours, I strongly disagree. I think Mr. Zecevic's arguments should go to the weight of this evidence, not its admissibility. He's identified the chief's name and signature on both those documents. If you look at them internally you can compare there are not dramatic differences as are being suggested by Mr. Zecevic. There's also an indication that a supplement was sent because the local SJB had not received specific guidance about the traffic report, I think. There's no doubt about the authenticity of these two reports. There may be some explanation that we don't yet have and can't get from this witness about why there's a difference, but I think that can be resolved by Your Honours reading them together and considering them in line with the testimony you've heard from this witness, from other documents in the case, and from other witness who have testified about what happened in Zvornik. I think it should be admitted in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I'm not sure I fully understood your objection. Are you saying that one of documents is but a draft that was never sort of adopted in the end and therefore should not be admitted, or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, that is precisely where the problem lies. That is to say, there are two documents that better same name, "Report of the public security station of Zvornik for 1992." Both documents are signed, both have an accompanying letter stating that they were sent to the centre of -- of security stations. So both documents pertain to an identical matter, that is to say this is a report of their work for 1992. These two documents bear different dates. One is dated December 1992 - excuse me - and the other one January 1993. Since both documents were submitted -- seemed to have been submitted, we don't know which one is the real and actual report on the work done, because as I've already said, and I say that again, they considerably differ in certain parts. In this situation we truly do not know what the true and actual report of the work of the SJB for 1992 is. That is the essence of my objection, because if you were to admit this document now completely as proposed by Mr. Hannis and through this witness who had never seen the document, who simply knows about certain facts, then we have a problem. You will have two documents in evidence issued by the same public security station, two documents that treat the same subject matter but that are different nevertheless. So I absolutely disagree with Mr. Hannis. We are not talking about the weight that you are going to give to certain evidence. It simply has to do with the authenticity of one of these documents. One of these documents must be the real report, but then the other one is not the real report. That is my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would have thought that authenticity would go to the veracity or the originality of the documents. The fact that there are inconsistencies between the two documents in terms of the facts that they deal with is not, in my view, an issue that challenges the authenticity of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, I absolutely do not agree. Actually, think about the following situation: You have a document that is called order of the minister of the interior and it has a certain number and a certain date. Then you have another document, order of the minister with a number and a date. The numbers are identical, the signatures are identical. However, both orders -- I mean, the two orders have different texts, completely different texts, and they treat the same problem. What do we do then? We have to decide which one of the two orders is valid. That is the situation that we have at hand now. You have two reports for 1992 of the public security station of Zvornik. If there are two reports, we have to establish -- or rather, the Prosecutor has to bring in a witness who would show or prove to us in some way which of the two reports is the right report, because obviously not both can be reports of the public security station, because they differ drastically, to my mind. It is that sense that we really do not know what the right and true report for 1992 is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, there are two -- there are two reports, two cover letters. The witness's -- the witness recognised the two signatures. So that goes for hypothesis that two reports were sent. As long as there is no shred of proof that there isn't but one sent, there has been sent two reports. And then we have two reports, haven't we? Whatever may be in it, that means that that person has sent two reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it can be understood that way. However, the witness only recognises signatures. He does not recognise either report because he hadn't seen any one of them. Since this is an official document, not two reports can be submitted as such. It is the obligation of the public security station to submit one report, one annual report. They cannot submit two or more reports. So one of these two reports is not the actual, the right report of that public security station, and we cannot establish that through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my learned friend keeps saying these reports differ drastically and significantly. He hasn't pointed to you anything where there's a drastic or significant difference. In addition, I think Judge Delvoie has it correctly. There's nothing to suggest why two reports couldn't have been sent. The first report is sent. The chief decides or discovers that something's been omitted or there's some additional information. He files a later report. But that's something that should not part admission of both reports, and Your Honours can sort it out later. His objections go to weight, not authenticity. He's not saying that these reports weren't written by the chief who's name and signature appear on there and whose name and signature have been confirmed by this witness as the man who was the chief at the time. They're both authentic. Now, he may have an argument about which was has validity, which one has weight, which one was the one that was deemed official, but the substantial portion of the contents of both are, in my view, from what I've read and seen, identical. I think it should come in, his arguments can go weight. We can ask questions of other witnesses later that may address it, but there's no reason that these can't come in now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you give me enough time, I can explain to you how come they differ. The first four questions that Mr. Hannis put to this witness and the excerpts that he read out to him and he indicated some parts of that particular report, they simply do not exist in the other report. That is definitely the situation. In addition to that, there are other differences between the two reports. What I have been saying is the following: Mr. Hannis is now asking us to speculate as to whether the chief of the public security station sent two reports or withdrew one or perhaps supplemented that report. We cannot speculate in that way. The problem is that as soon as there are two reports, for me there is the question of authenticity of one of the said reports. We have to know which one of the two is the official report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We are satisfied that the reports are admissible. At the end of the day it will be for the Chamber to decide what weight to attach to either or both of the reports. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, I'd like to show you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The report will become Exhibit P348, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, could I show the witness next 65 ter number 2771.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, did you know Risto Zaric?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And tell us again who he was and where he worked.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Risto Zaric worked in state security, and to this day he works in the state security of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, 2771 is a state security report or an official note prepared based on information received from Risto Zaric. This document is a companion similar to 2770, which now is Exhibit Number P321. That was an official note prepared by the same author as the author of this one based on information from Brano Grujic. You'll recall this is one of the documents for which the Republic of Serbia had requested protective measures concerning the identity of the author, and therefore I argued concerning the one regarding Mr. Grujic that authenticity should not be an issue for this document. It's a document that we received pursuant to an RFA, a request for assistance, to the government of Serbia. It was delivered to us, and then they approached this court and made requests for certain protective measures regarding the document. I would suggest that's sufficient evidence to satisfy you that the document is authentic, because otherwise the government wouldn't be taking that position, and therefore, now that you have some information from this witness confirming that Risto Zaric was a member of the national security working in Zvornik at the time, those two things together I think are sufficient for me now to tender this document as a contemporaneous report about what was happening in Zvornik from someone who was present with knowledge. And I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, this document is not on the list OTP provided us with, the list of documents for use with ST-196.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe it was, Your Honour. I'm checking. It's on my copy of the list that was sent to, I think, Ms. Featherstone and Defence counsel on -- I see Mr. Zecevic seems to be confirming. It was not in numerical order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's not in numerical order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's the last one on the list I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I see. Yeah. Sorry, that's why I overlooked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My apologies. It was a late addition and so it ended up at the end instead of its appropriate place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we object to having this document admitted into evidence through this witness because we see no nexus whatsoever between this witness and the document that is being proffered. The fact that the witness knows the purported author of this document does not mean that he knows anything else concerning this report, any facts contained in the report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, could you assist us on this nexus issue? The question of authenticity doesn't arise. The nexus?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the content of this report is some information about Zuco and his unit but also some information about the identity of various members of the paramilitaries who were operating in Zvornik at the time. Given Mr. Zaric's position in the state security at Zvornik, it seems to me a logical inference to be drawn is that that's the kind of information he would know about. That is the kind of information that the state security people would be trying to keep track of, and, therefore, I think that gives us the nexus for you to have sufficient confidence that the official note contains information from a person who would likely have that information, and therefore you can accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Information that the witness would know about? Shouldn't you ask him at least some question about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can ask him to review the list of names and if he recognises any of those names as members of the volunteers and formations that he saw operating in Zvornik. I know, for example, at page 6 of the English you already have information that Rade Tanackovic was a member of Zuco's group. That's in this document. I think there are some others. Pivarski is listed here, some of the others that you're already familiar with. I don't know that this witness can advance us much further upon that, and I don't know that he needs to, frankly, Your Honour. That's my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Tendered, admitted, and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P349, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Lastly, Witness, the three documents I'd like to show you very quickly, 30 -- 65 ter number 3214, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would indicate I don't have an English translation of these next three documents at this point in time. I'll explain in a moment. I only have a translation of the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, did you have an opportunity to see this document during your proofing?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a telegram, dispatch. Yes, yes. From the communications centre. Yes. Dispatches were sent that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And does this appear to be one of the communication logbooks for Zvornik SJB?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The numbers go from 1 and onwards. This is the logbook of outgoing dispatches. Yes. That was the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness 3215, 65 ter 3215.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I'm just wondering the relevance of this document which is right now on our monitors. It says here the 9th of January, 1979. 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, these logbooks cover extensive periods of time. We can certainly make an excerpt for the period late 1991 through 1992, and we'll do that. But the logbook came as a whole. We didn't feel it appropriate for us to tear it apart, at the beginning at least. Also, there may be some argument to be made from prior years' communications versus the level of communications during late 1991 and 1992 during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I understand. I now withdraw my objection. I was just wondering, because I still didn't have the time to see the whole lot. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Hannis, you have to be more helpful to the Chamber. I have no idea about what this logbook really shows. Is that a list over outgoing telegrams from the Zvornik SJB? And in that case, telegrams to whom? And -- and in what connection? We are completely at a loss here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just want to mark these for identification at this point in time. But this witness has been able to look at them and say that he recognises these as communication logbooks of some sort from the Zvornik SJB. At this time all I want to do is mark them for identification, and later on I'm hoping through other evidence we'll be able to explain what they are and why they're relevant in this case. By showing a particular entry that will be a number of a telegram, hopefully we'll have a hard copy of it or we'll have a hard copy of a document that made reference to having received that particular item. I believe those are links that can be made, but I can't make them with this witness at this time, but he is the one who has looked at the books and said, These look like the Zvornik logbooks that were in Zvornik in 1992. He's just my foundation witness for that purpose, and because that's all he can talk about, all I want to do is ask him about that and mark them for identification for right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So what's the Prosecution -- the Defence's position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We're not objecting. We understand the -- I understand now what is the position of Prosecution. We don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P350, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And quickly if we could show the witness 3215. 65 ter 3215.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Witness, this is one of the three books that you had a chance to look at during your proofing.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise it as one of the communication logbooks for Zvornik SJB?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the 12th of November 1991. It says that this was received from the B and H MUP, and it sayings who received it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we mark that one for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P351, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And lastly if we could show the witness 65 ter 3211. We did have an English translation of the first page, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, this English translation says this is the expedited log of outgoing open telegrams for 1991.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise this book as also being one of the communication logs for Zvornik SJB?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May we mark this one for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, this one seems to be specific in terms of a year, 1991. Is that a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think there are some telegrams in late 1991 that may be relevant for our purposes, and I believe -- again, I believe there are some that actually go beyond 1991 in this logbook. If we could go to the last page, perhaps we could see a date to confirm if my memory's correct. If we could go back one page perhaps. I think this date is 5 April 1992, if I follow the sequence in the logbook correctly, Your Honour. I can't go to the precise page now, but I believe that's correct, they are sequential. You'll see this is number 1346, so I think it is 1991 going into 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber's being asked to take on faith your tentative view on this matter, but inasmuch as you are asking for it to be marked, and I hear no objection, I suppose we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for accepting me on that, Your Honour. I can look at my hard copy quickly, but I'm pretty sure that it did transfer from 1991 to 1992. I see at page 61 in this -- in the B/C/S of this document, you see the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992. Page 63 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P352, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thanks to my case manager, and thank you, Your Honours, and I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Panic.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In early 1992 -- or, rather, towards the end of 1991, you were the reserve police commander, as you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was assistant commander of the reserve station, and that was since the 1st of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can I just ask you one thing. Since this has to be translated, please wait for me to finish before you start your answer. Thank you. The police reserve was mobilised on the 1st of September, 1991, on the orders of the then minister, Alija Mustafic, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That would mean that according to the estimate of the then MUP in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because I think that this order pertained to the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in my view, that indicated that the situation was already very tense at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that this had to do with the war going on in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that in this case it has been no dispute over the fact that the SJB Zvornik was divided on the 6th of April. However, if I understood your testimony here properly, it was evident that this separation was inevitable, even before that date.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said that it was either on the 23rd or 24th March the deputy Adnan Karovic mobilised only the Muslim policemen, surrounded the SUP building, and provided security for it. When we learned about this, we asked for a meeting to be held. An inspector came from Tuzla. I can't remember his name at the moment. And we had this meeting, and we agreed how to proceed. However, I think that it was on the 3rd or 4th April in the village of Sapna a column of soldiers and some Muslim extremists, if I may call them that, because there was no proper army there, they killed a warrant officer second class and killed another soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You spoke about this already. Let us now go back. I'm going to ask you questions so that we can be more expeditious. Adnan Karovic, the assistant commander who, as you said, on or around 23rd or 24th of March called upon the Muslim members of the MUP to provide security of the SJB, and he omitted to call up the Serb officers. Before that, was he for -- on a sick leave for a year?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not an assistant. He was a deputy commander, to begin with. And maybe a year before that or maybe even more he had come from a special unit in Belgrade, and he was on a prolonged sick leave at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Serb members of the SJB resented this move of his?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that is why we asked for a meeting to be held. That's why this inspector came. We asked for even the minister to come, but an official from Tuzla came.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And if I understood you correctly, at that meeting you wanted an explanation why this was done in that manner and why only Muslims were called up and why they surrounded the SJB. You wanted answers. However, since that failed, you left this meeting in protest. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First we left, but then someone persuaded to us come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, this inspector from Tuzla joined you and left the meeting because he also wanted to hear some answers.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was clear to you already at the time that the division of the SUP was something that was inevitable?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was clear to us, but we nevertheless hoped that all these disagreements could be ironed out, that the chief of the centre would come to talk to us and that we would be able to continue working together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The then SJB chief was Osman Mustafic. He was a professional policeman.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He was an SDA candidate, but do you know that the SDS was the one who supported him and that he didn't have the support of his own SDA party?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Alic Asim, or Asim Alic?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He had come from Belgrade some five or six months before that and before the outbreak of the conflict he was the assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He was Dragan Spasojevic's assistant; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the night between the 3rd or 4th April, apart from the incident in Sapna, the weapons from the public security station in Zvornik was distributed to Muslims -- or, rather, to the Green Berets? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was stories going around at the time that on that evening when they surrounded the SUP that weapons were being distributed. However, all those senior officers were in the depot, including the chief, and I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Patriotic League, as an illegal armed formation in Zvornik, was established in that town on the 26th of July, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the exact date, but I know that both this organisation and the Green Berets were established in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that approximately at that time on Mount Godus a Green Beret unit was formed, and there is even a monument standing there now? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that there is a monument now. I didn't go there before. I heard stories, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the time when the Patriotic League was formed and Green Berets as, shall we say, illegal armed formations of the Party of Democratic Action, that the Muslims also had set up a Crisis Staff? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about this Crisis Staff, but I don't know who was on it. I know that Asim Zuber was the president of the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Sakib Halilovic, aka Kibe?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was appointed commander of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that every village in the municipality after July 1991 following the formation of the Patriotic League as an illegal armed formation for Zvornik, that each village in this municipality that was populated by Muslim received a plan of deployment and engagement?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing in particular about that. I only heard about that. We did nothing about that, because no orders were received to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you -- have you ever heard of Captain Almir who commanded the Muslim units? He was from Kula Grad, and he was fighting there in April 1992 for about three weeks.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he had come to Zvornik way back in December 1991 in order to set up military units, to arm them, to train them, and to build fortifications?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Maybe senior officers knew about this, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this Muslim Crisis Staff and members of those units had a plan designed to blow up the dam?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that, but it's possible. I heard about the Crveni Mulj dam and that some preparations were made, but I personally didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that another Crisis Staff was formed at the level of the municipality? The former one that we discussed was the war Crisis Staff set up by the Patriotic League. However, there was another Crisis Staff headed by Abdulah Pasic, the president of the municipality of the time. Mustafic was there. The defence was covered by Alija Kapicic [phoen]. There was also --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slowly read the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I heard about that, and I heard about that there was a rift that took place there. There were different factions, and there were some personal clashes between all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know by any chance when this Crisis Staff of theirs was established, approximately?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this Crisis Staff had introduced a curfew in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not officially, but there were some stories going around that these reserve Muslim policemen had green berets, that when they were working there they put their green berets on and that they were patrolling the streets, but I don't know anything in particular about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, when you reach a convenient point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have just two more questions, and I've finished with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you know that a Serbian Crisis Staff that proclaimed the state of war was also set up?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How long after the establishment of that was -- or how long after the 8th of April was the interim government established?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I wasn't involved in either the Crisis Staff or the interim government. Therefore, I have no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's convenient at this point to adjourn. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honours, we are joined by Mr. Cvijetic in this session. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And my I just add, welcome back into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Panic, let us move on to the 6th of April. On the 6th of April, the members of the MUP who were of Serb ethnicity separated from the SJB Zvornik and went to Karakaj. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Zecevic please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mijic, who was a judge at the time, proclaims himself chief of MUP. Mr. Mijic, who was a judge at the time, is proclaimed chief of the MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He worked in court, but it wasn't on the 6th of April that he was appointed or proclaimed the chief of the Serbian station, but it was a bit before that. That's when he just took over that duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Dragan Spasojevic is the commander; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Spasojevic also worked for the police a bit over a year.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He worked while there was a joint SUP there, but when Mustafic Osman was appointed chief, he was appointed commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In professional terms he was a medical technician; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I think that he studied economics in Greece.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that you said that he studied economics in the town of Brcko, not --

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of April, you were established in the Alhos building; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Members of the paramilitaries came there, Arkan's men, and Seselj's men, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We found some of them there and others arrived when they got out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that you stated somewhere that some of them wore blue camouflage uniforms of the MUP of Serbia and that they even had rank insignia on the uniforms and that a certain Peja had the rank insignia of a general; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they did have some kind of rank insignia. I'm not sure it was that of a general, but that's what they called him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These were certainly significantly different uniforms from the ones that you had and that you were issued and that you wore?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were blue with a bit of a whitish pattern, newer ones, and the material, the fabric, was of higher quality. Things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, do you not know whether these were official uniforms of the MUP of Serbia, or do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. We assumed, since they had come from Serbia and said that they were members of Arkan's unit, that they belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: During the fighting in Zvornik on the 8th of April, you, that is to say the active-duty members of the police, did not take part in any fighting; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your assignment was to hold certain check-points and secure certain vital points in town; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After this unit, Arkan's unit entered town. We followed them on buses, and by every important landmark two or three policemen would be assigned to be on guard duty here or there, depending on the landmark involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Panic, that check-points existed in 1991 as well? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, on the bridge and facing Serbia, and I think on Vidakova Njiva as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These check-points in 1991, of course that was at the time while there was still a joint MUP, and they were set up. These check-points were set up on orders from your then chief -- or, rather, I assume that it was done on the orders of the BH MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, most of them were joint checkpoints. One policeman would, say, be a Muslim, and the other one a Serb. So it was the end of 1991, there were check-points around residential buildings so that the actual residents would be sort of guarding the building involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this was some kind of self-organisation of the people. This had nothing to do with the police; right? I mean the guarding of these residential buildings.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know of the action called Punkt 91 where the police together with the army, the JNA, held check-points in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was that the case where you were?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I know that there was a company of the army that was deployed and training reservists in Celopek and another in Branjevo, but the police, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, these check-points in 1991 that you held, you say one was at the bridge and the other one was, I don't know where exactly, in the territory of Zvornik. What did the police do at these check-points? Did they ask people to show IDs? Did they take weapons from people and the like?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was primarily done by the traffic people. These were traffic controls. Already then there were traffic checks in Mali Zvornik opposite us, and where we were vehicles were checked to see what they were transporting, because at that time people were already saying that weapons were being transported. So, yes, that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would be interested in the following: These check-points from 1991 that were held at that time, did they significantly differ in any way from the check-points in 1992, that were established by the police in 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This was a regular service, as it were, in the joint organs in 1991. It is possible that somewhere in some villages there were some check-points where -- that we did not know about when Serb or Muslim citizens would organise some kind of self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You do not understand what I'm saying. I'm not interested in the composition --

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- of the employees who were at the check-points. I'm interested in the way they acted and how they exercised their authority in 1991 and in 1992. Was there any difference involved?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991 it was mostly checks of persons and goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And regular police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 there were checks of the population that was moving. For example, if it was a Serb check-point, they would check where Muslims were going, then they were given permits and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, in 1991 at check-points people were supposed to show their IDs; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, this was just in order to know who these persons were and where they were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So after the 8th of April you were providing security at facilities, and you held these check-points for the most part, and as far as I understood what you said in your testimony yesterday, on the 2nd or 3rd day you actually withdrew from Zvornik and you went to Celopek because you thought it was safer there.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You went to Celopek because these troops that took part in the takeover of Zvornik, the paramilitaries, as we've been calling them here, and that is what they were, because they had withdrawn; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We heard that the Crisis Staff had had a quarrel with Arkan's and Seselj's men, that they withdrew to Radaljska Banja, to Mali Zvornik. And then we saw the TO withdrew from the check-point facing Devic, and we decided to cross the bridge to Mali Zvornik. We went to Alhos and from Alhos to Celopek.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In fact. At that moment Zvornik remained --

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Empty. Do you know, perhaps, or have you heard perhaps what this quarrel was all about between the Crisis Staff and the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Some said it had to do with payments, others that it had to do with disagreements in combat operations. I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Payment? Payments for their participation?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at a moment on the 9th and 10th, how many of you active police members were there who had gone through police training, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of Serb ethnicity? Either 24 or 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this document, 65 ter 2121. That is a document dated the 21st of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the record, I believe that has an exhibit number now, P325.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you see it, Mr. Panic?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You have, therefore, had a look at this document. You see that on the 21st of April -- well, this is a list of active policemen of the milicija on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it was signed by Milos Pantelic, the then chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the document scrolled down a bit. Could you please scroll the document down just a little bit so that the witness could see the signature. [In English] I'm sorry, could we have the documents lowered down so the witness can see the -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see that this was signed by Milos Pantelic; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It seems --

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the 21st of April. So two days later there were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Speakers are overlapping. It is impossible to follow two speakers at the same time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, please just wait for my question to finish and then answer it.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. I don't know when the interpretation is over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Look at the transcript and when the letters stop, then you can start answering.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, after a while yet another paramilitary group showed up, and you called them Gogic's men. When did they roughly arrive in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They arrived -- well, I found out about that later. I didn't -- well, they came towards the beginning. They entered Zvornik. However, for a while they went somewhere. I don't know whether it was in the territory of the municipality of Zvornik or they returned to Loznica, but yet again they came back when Milos Pantelic came to become chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That was sometime in -- sometime in mid-may; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then when they came, the then chief, Pantelic, and his -- Vasilic, Marinko Vasilic was the commander at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The two of them, Milos Pantelic and Marinko Vasilic, I assume, with the support of this transitional government in Zvornik proclaimed these men of Gogic's as MUP members; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were attached and they were given uniforms of MUP members and they received salaries from the MUP as well. Well, they were on the same payroll that we were on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So there is this one group of people who came from Serbia, and the chief, with the support of the transitional government, dresses them up in uniforms, attaches them to the MUP, and he gives them some kind of powers so that they can do police work.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And he places them on the same payroll that you were on as active policemen, as true members of the MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This transitional government paid salaries to you and them; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After a while, these men of Gogic's actually start doing police work, whereas you real policemen, active-duty policemen, are sent -- I mean you as true MUP officials, you are sent to the front line; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So that was the reason why you had conflict and the fact that you rebelled against this Marinko Vasilic.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was our dissatisfaction because we were not actually doing what was our job, whereas persons who were not properly trained for that kind of work stayed in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have just received a suggestion from my colleague that there is an erroneous recording of your answer. Line 49. I asked you the following: After a while these men of Gogic's actually started doing police work, whereas you real policemen, active-duty policemen, policemen who were true MUP officials, you were sent to the front line; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, these men of Gogic's, if I can put it this way, they were individuals who were on the brink or perhaps outlaws as such.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them, I think. Even from prison. And quite a few of them had been at the Croatian front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We will get back to that later. I would now like to show you several documents. These are documents that you discussed with my colleague yesterday. The first one, P329.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it please be called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My colleague put questions to you about this document, and he wasn't interested in its substance that much. He was interested in the date and the signature, whereas the contents of the document are precisely what I'm interested in, and I'd like us to discuss that. I have a very poor image on my monitor. It's all in blue. I don't know what the case is with you, Mr. Panic.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can barely make something out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have the document in hard copy? I would appreciate very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may be able to read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will now receive a hard copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I would need also 330 and 331, P330 and 31. Thank you. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, Mr. Panic. You have reviewed the document yesterday. Can you please focus on the substance for a moment. This is a daily report from the Zvornik municipality public security station and was sent to the CSB Bijeljina, which was supposed to forward it on to the CSB in Sarajevo. The document relates to the 2nd of June, 1992. It was signed by Chief Milos Pantelic. The only event that was of interest to the security situation mentioned in the document is the event in the villages of Kovacevici and Vitnica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at P330 now. This is another document that you've also looked at. The usher will provide with you a hard copy now. We will see ours on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add something? The report says there were combat activities in the villages of Kovacevici and Vitnica between the Muslim extremists and members the Serbian army. Nowhere in this document is it stated that a police unit was involved and participated in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Right. My question had to do with something else. Please look at P330 now. This is a document bearing a subsequent date. You've also reviewed it yesterday. It is again a report from the Zvornik public security station which states that it should be sent to Sarajevo through the Bijeljina CSB, and it relates to the 3rd of June, 1992. Again it was signed by Chief Pantelic. The event for the 3rd of June mentioned here was the one that took place in the settlement of Djevanje. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us also look at P331, which is a daily report for the 4th of June. This is another document you reviewed yesterday. You can see that it is a daily report on current events of interest to the security situation in the area covered by the Zvornik SJB, and the request is that it be sent to Sarajevo through the Bijeljina CSB. The document states that in the past 24 hours there had been no combat operations or, rather, events of interest to security; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that the Prosecutor showed you another one dated the 7th of June, 1992, which relates to that same date and which also states that there had been no events of interest to security. Let me ask you this: In the course of your testimony, you stated that on the 1st of June, 1992, on the orders of Marinko Vasilic, you went to Bijelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bijeli Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Bijeli Potok. You were tasked with assisting in the process of placing individuals of Muslim ethnicity on buses in order for them to be transported to Memici, which was under the control of the Muslim forces. All this was a follow-up on an agreement reached by politicians as explained to you on that same day by Vasilic when he tasked you with it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Roughly how many, in your view, were transported on these trucks?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless I'm mistaken, between 5 to 6.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At a later date you learnt that the exchange had been organised for allegedly 4.000 Serbs who had been held at a stadium in Tuzla and that this prompted the exchange exercise. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt subsequently that around 700 men had been detained at the technical centre in order to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. That was not my question. What I'm asking you about is that it seems to me that you said at one point that you subsequently learnt in Belgrade, in the course of the testimony of another witness, that the exchange had been prompted by the fact that 4.000 Serbs had been detained at the stadium in Tuzla and that for that reason the Serbs were supposed to be exchanged for the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Marinko Vasilic said at the trial in Belgrade that in the staff he had learned that the 700 individuals which were detained in the technical centre were supposed to be exchanged for the individuals held at the stadium at Tuzla, whereas it did not involve the women and children who had already been transported to Memici. It didn't have anything to do with them. It had to do with these roughly 700 individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Thank you for this clarification. These 700 individuals who were supposed to be exchanged were taken to the technical school at Karakaj, which, as you've already explained, was under the control of the Karakaj company.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your testimony at page 36, lines 19 and 20, states that when it came to Potok you were standing by the truck and you heard shooting. However, the army which was this charge of the action did not allow you to approach the area. Rather, you were told to remain by the truck.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not that they did not allow me to approach the area. Rather, as I moved to get there, they told me to stay away because the army was engaged in shooting above the school. And since I didn't have the authority to be there, I went back to my place and some four or five days later I heard that five or six individuals had been killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On that evening you returned and reported to Marinko Vasilic about having completed your task. You said that Miko Miljanovic was present there as well. I think this is what you said yesterday; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday at page 38, lines 19 to 25, you said that two to three days later you heard that at the time when you were present in Bijeli Potok the army had killed five or six Muslim civilians. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And at that point I tied in the shooting that I had witnessed with this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your testimony yesterday was that in that same period, that's to say, two to three days after the 1st of June, you heard that mass-scale murders were taking place at the technical school in Karakaj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that individuals were being taken out by trucks to Klanac --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: To the slaughter house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... and that that's where murders were being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say the slaughterhouse, you're referring to that --

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Gero's Slaughterhouse. That's the slaughterhouse that belonged to Gero Salihovic, I believe. It was in the field by the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
