utterances.text: In the course of these two or three days the 4 or 5.000 Muslims were being transported, 700 individuals were detained at the school in Karakaj in order to be exchanged, five or six civilians were killed on the 1st of June by the army in Bijeli Potok, and mass-scale killings were taking place at the technical school in Karakaj and partly at the slaughterhouse. At the same time as we were to see from the reports sent by Marinko Vasilic, there were no events taking place of security interest, save for the 2nd or the 3rd, I believe, where he said some fighting took place. However, nowhere does he mention any of the facts that we were able to establish right now, thanks to you, and which happened precisely during that period and in the way in which you described. Tell me, in your opinion is it possible that these would not be -- or that this would not be information of security interest?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't presume so, but he stated the same even before during the Belgrade trial, that as soon as he learnt that the army was involved and that the whole process was aimed at exchanging people, he did not take any steps because did he not believe that he should interfere. Since it was the army that brought them over there, that guarded them, and since the objective of the exercise was the exchange, he didn't have a part to play in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If that is the explanation, then how can we account for the fact that he is reporting about combat activities, which evidently involved the army, but omitted to report on these events which are definitely of security interest since civilians were victims at the hands of the army, since mass-scale killings were taking place, since large numbers of individuals were being transported to Muslim-held areas? I don't see how these facts cannot be of security interest. I'm not interested in Vasilic's opinion. I'm interested in yours. Based on your experience as a policeman, is this information the sort of information that would be considered of security interest and which should be reported to the CSB or not?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under all the rules that were in force previously and now, they would be of security interest. And I'm referring to the rules that existed before the war and during the war. They -- this sort of information would have to be reported. I don't know whether this was an agreement or an instruction from the army that this sort of information should not be reported on. This is something I don't know. All the officers were aware of it. The barracks was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So this information was not passed on. We have here the bulletins of daily events in this case file relating to those dates. Those were compiled by the Ministry of the Interior, and of course no events that we mention now do feature in those reports. I suppose you haven't seen these bulletins.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't even seen those who were sent. The chief would just designate this to be sent to the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: For reference, I would like to just say to this Trial Chamber that I'm talking about the bulletin dated the 3rd of June, 1992, on daily events compiled by the MUP. It's 65 ter 971. The same one dated 4th of June. That's 65 ter 972. The one dated the 5th of June is 65 ter 1019. And the one dated the 7th of June is 65 ter 973.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to those documents, I don't know if there's a motion to admit them. Now, do I have an objection about foundation. They're typed. I don't see a signature. I don't see anything other than a three-digit number. And given the fact that the reports from the Zvornik SJB were being sent to Bijeljina with a request that they be forwarded to Sarajevo, the fact that a report for events on the 3rd of June may not have appeared in the bulletin from Sarajevo on the 4th is not necessarily significant because there may have been a delay in Bijeljina receiving it and then forwarding it on to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This -- these daily reports mention which reports have not been received up to the -- up to the point when the -- when the daily report of the MUP was created, and they list not received from, let's say, CSB Trebinje, not received from CSB Banja Luka. But in all these cases it is evident that they received the reports from CSB Bijelina in all these. That's why I think it's relevant, and I wanted -- we can show -- we can show the documents to the witness if Your Honours pleases. I don't -- I don't see the problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't think it will help to show it to this witness because I don't think he can comment on that. But in 971 and 972, maybe it's not in the English translation, but I don't see anything indicating that a report was received from CSB Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the -- at the very end, the last paragraph of all reports usually contains the reports from the following CSBs have not been received. In case it doesn't, then -- then it means that all reports have been received. If you check --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'm looking at --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... the daily bulletins --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm looking at what's translated as daily report number 101, dated the 3rd of June in Sarajevo, the last paragraph says, "The centre has not received security reports from the following SJBs ..." And I don't see Zvornik on there, and I don't see reference --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's exactly my point. What I'm trying to say is that obviously they received the report from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, but given the evidence about Zvornik and the difficulties in transmitting communications to Sarajevo at this point in time, the report from Zvornik about that date may have been delayed by a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, if the report had been delayed and was not received in the MUP on that particular date, then they would list at the very end that they haven't received the report from Zvornik. If they haven't listed as missing, it's obvious that they received it. The point of the matter is that the report, which we saw -- which you showed to the witness before and I showed the witness today does not contain these information which this witness was testifying about and which his superior who was supposed to transfer this information did not. That is -- that is the point. And I believe these daily bulletins were offered as Prosecution exhibits. I don't -- I don't understand why you are objecting to admission of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm hoping they will be, but I think we need more foundation about them to get them in at this point, unless Defence is willing to stipulate that these are the official reports from the republican MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, with all due respect, I believe these four reports have a much bigger nexus with the testimony of this client -- this witness and the -- and the documents which have been shown to him than some of the documents we have been admitted previously during the direct examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my concern is that the argument being made based on this document is not necessarily supported by the evidence so far. Exhibit P329 is the report from Chief Pantelic, dated the 3rd of June from Zvornik. We don't know what time of day that was sent. The report -- daily report number 101, which is 65 ter 971 is dated 3 June in Sarajevo. I don't know if that report was written at 6.00 in the morning on the 3rd of June or at midnight. So if it was written 6.00 in the morning, that may have been written before P329 was sent from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Surely, Mr. Hannis, you would not dispute that in case the report came late, it would be reported on the 4th, and we offered the 4th as well. So as it's not contained in the 4th, the report for the 4th June, it is obvious that both reports were received at the time when they were received, and they didn't contain anything, as we saw that they don't contain any kind of information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zecevic is talking about 65 ter 0972, which purports to be daily report number 117. That's the day following what was listed as daily report number 101. I don't know if there are 16 reports between June 3rd and June the 4th. That's why I have some question about the foundation and authenticity of these particular exhibits. Also this one dated June the 4th, I don't see anywhere in it where it listed which municipalities they received reports from and which they didn't. There seem to be no reference. And finally, I would say Exhibit 65 ter 1019, which the Defence is proposing to send, does contain on page 4 of the English translation information from the Bijeljina CSB which contains information about the 2 June events in the village of Kovacevici and Liplje, where two soldiers were killed and five were wounded. So that indicates that if it's coming through Bijeljina CSB, there's at least a three- or four-day delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely why we offered 65 ter 973, which is the 7th of June, so in order to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will admit them and have them marked as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Should I read the -- again the documents? 65 ter 971, 972, 973, and 1019.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will become Exhibits 1D68, 1D69, 1D70, and 1D71, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, sorry, but this is the procedure we have to follow. Can you please look at document 65 ter 89. That's an order -- or, rather, an instruction issued by the Ministry of the Interior on the 18th of April, 1992. It was distributed to all CSBs within the ministry of Republika Srpska. That means Sarajevo, Banja Luka, Trebinje, Bijelina, and Doboj. Please look at this document. It's 150/92, dated 18th of April. It has been ordered that all daily reports and all other security related events are sent by telefax to certain numbers, and it was signed by the minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You as an experienced police officer, know that the duty of sending daily periodical and annual report was something that was always there in the police and will always be part of the police work?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. It probably reached the desk of the chief, but as you say, from experience I know that reports must be sent about any significant event.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have -- [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D72.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Panic, let's go back to the issue of the chief. You said that Mr. Mijic remained in his position for about six weeks, that is to say the chief of the Zvornik SJB, and that after that the Crisis Staff appointed Milos Pantelic to that post; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then for a while Spasojevic carried out this duty as an acting commander and then he was replaced by Marinko Vasilic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that yesterday when my learned colleague Mr. Hannis was questioning you, it was established that Mr. Marinko Vasilic became chief on the night between the 8th and 9th of June; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And he remained chief all the way to 27th of July when eventually the minister and the Ministry of the Interior appointed the chief of the Zvornik public security station which was Mico Lokancevic. And from then on you started functioning in a sort of normal way, because on that day all these paramilitary units were either expelled or arrested; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just add to -- a couple of things. On the 27th of July, he resigned, but he remained there until the 2nd of August. Mico came on the 2nd of August, and that is when the hand-over of duty took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was exactly intending to show you the documents 65 ter 335, which pertains to this. While we are waiting, let me ask you this. Mr. Mico Lokancevic, if I understood you correctly, was a police officer and used to work before the war at the Kalesija SJB. Then he came to Zvornik towards the end of July or early August in 1992 for the first time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When he came to take over the duty of the chief, that's when he came there first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you saw this document -- or, rather, this minutes. That's P341.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You saw it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This record refers to the hand-over of duty which is completely consistent with the law and the rules as far as you know.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Whenever there is a hand-over of duty between two chiefs, both before the war and thereafter, this kind of record would be made; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And here you see that there were listed here members of the commission who carried out this hand-over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You testified yesterday about this on page 51, lines 16 to 19. Essentially, until the appointment of Mico Lokancevic as the chief of the MUP, all the previous chiefs starting from the beginning of April were appointed by either the Crisis Staff or the interim government -- government; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As an experienced police officer, you know that under normal circumstances the chief of the public security station is normally appointed by the minister of interior at the recommendation or proposal of the chief of the SJB. Can we now see document 65 ter 96, please. I'm sorry, your answer was not recorded to my last question. I asked you as an experienced police officer you know that under normal circumstances the chief of the public security station is appointed by the ministry of the -- minister of the interior at the proposal of the S -- of CSB centre, and I think you replied affirmatively to this question. Is that right? What's your answer?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I do apologise, but yes, you see, we have to deal with this slowly so that everything can be interpreted. I'm not all that skillful yet. Number 96. That's the 65 ter number of the document I requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just giving the witness time to read the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see this document, this is a decision of the minister of the interior, dated the 25th of April, and it refers to the law on state administration and the Law on Internal Affairs, the relevant provisions of the law, and in paragraph 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the document scrolled down a bit so that you can have a look. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 it says that chiefs of centres of security services are duty bound to obtain prior approval of the minister of the interior before employees are designated to the following jobs. Bullet point number 3 inter alia that is chief of CSB. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the document scrolled down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will see that it is signed by the minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic. Tell me, Mr. Panic, to the best of your knowledge as an experienced policeman, is this the way things were usually done, that the minister has to give his approval for the appointment of chiefs of public security stations; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it was before, and it is only natural that that is the way it is today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a number -- or, rather, I would like to tender this document into evidence. It is the decision of the Ministry of the Interior, dated the 25th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D73, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, if you're about to move on to something else, this is the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. Okay, thank you very much. [Interpretation] Thank you. Now we're going to have a break, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Panic, yesterday the Prosecutor showed you and you commented on a document P338, and in that document it's a report of inspector Dragan Andan -- Dragomir Andan, that is, and Danilo Vuckovic made at the SJB Brcko and the SJB Zvornik and partly at the SJB Bijeljina between the 29th of May and the 12th of June, and the Prosecutor read to you something from page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please see page 4 on the screen. P338.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We'll just wait a little bit. Do you remember that you commented on this document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at page 4, which Mr. Hannis read to you. Page 4, pease, the first paragraph. Mr. Hannis read out to you one sentence and then he skipped one, whereas I would like us to read the sentence that was left out. It says here, beginning with: "Namely, the police employees are directly providing physical security of facilities that are of vital importance and otherwise important in the area of the Zvornik municipality, then there was an attempt to find a solution through the government, but there was no understanding." Mr. Panic, when one says facilities of vital importance and other facilities, one means primarily, I suppose, hospitals, the post office building, the municipal building, the radio transformer station, and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They do not have in mind anything like detention centres or prisons or collection centres?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, because the prison wardens and the security guards at prisons were specially appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say they were appointed specially, yesterday you looked at a document whereby a decision of the Crisis Staff, some of the reservists were transferred to Territorial Defence. These were police reservists. Do you remember that document?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, is the thesis well founded that some of those police reservists who were resubordinated to the Territorial Defence were involved in securing some of these facilities? I mean, the prisons and prison facilities.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning when the prisons were established, it was only the military and the paramilitary forces and the Territorial Defence that secured them. So before the army was constituted, at the beginning the prisons were established and only the military police secured them. And then later on the active-duty policemen took over that duty from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us comment events that took place in late July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the witness 65 ter 311.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this document, Mr. Panic. It's a document from the security services centre in Bijeljina, dated the 20th of July, 1992, and it's information on the security situation on the territory of Zvornik Serb municipality. Dragan Adnan was appointed chief of the CSB Bijeljina after the report of the 17th of June, 1992, which we just saw. At that moment, some problems in the operation of the Ministry of the Interior in the territory of the CSB Bijeljina territory, especially in Bijeljina and Brcko, were pointed out, and here he reviews the security situation in the territory of the Zvornik municipality. And he lists here three paramilitary units, Zuco, Pivarski, and Niski. Can you see that here in the middle of the text, in the middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And later on in the last paragraph on the first page he says that Zuco's unit numbers around 100 men armed with infantry weapons, and they also have heavy machine-guns and three anti-aircraft missiles built onto trucks. Do you confirm this information which was sent?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They also had three-barrel guns that were also installed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If we could please move on to the last page now, the last page of this document so that you can see the conclusion. Can you see the last paragraph of this conclusion? It says here: "We estimate that the current activity of these paramilitary units might cause great consequences for the security of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik. And in order to prevent this, we suggest that a special unit of the Republika Srpska MUP be deployed on the territory of Zvornik in order to eliminate all paramilitary formations, to strengthen the legal authorities and create conditions for the stabilising of the security situation on the above territory." So you've seen this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This was sent to the minister of the interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the under secretary of the national security service. Please tell me, I saw in the transcript yesterday that there was again something not clear about the status of the special unit of the MUP. That was the special brigade of the MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Milenko Karisik who was at the head of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that special brigade of the MUP was, let me put it that way, a special MUP unit which is linked to the seat of the MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And such a unit also existed in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It also existed previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it still exists today, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this special brigade of the Ministry of the Interior performs Special Police tasks in the territory where the need arises for it to be engaged and when there are such problems with which the local units and public security stations or centres, security services centres, cannot handle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are trained for that kind of work. They are also technically equipped, whereas ordinary policemen are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And as I understood your testimony until now, that was the situation that were faced with in Zvornik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us recall, the active-duty policemen were less than 30 in number, and only Zuca's group numbered more than 100 members; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. More than 100 members, because local criminals were also joining them, and they were not even registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So as I understood your testimony, they were not only more numerous, but they were also better armed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said so. I said earlier that they were armed. They had three-barrel guns. They even tried to make an armoured train in Glinica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document, this report dated the 20th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D74, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, the next document is P339. You had a look at that yesterday with my learned friend. This is also a dispatch made by Dragomir Andan and sent to the Ministry, dated 23rd of July, 1992, so three days after the previous report. And here again he reports in detail about the existence of the paramilitary units. And in addition to Zuco, Pivarski, and Niski there's also a Simo Chetnik who has 30 men under him. You can see that here, and he lists the weapons that they have; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And also the locations where they are operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We can see that some of them even have four Maljutka launchers.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the report says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the second page, please. First paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please see the next page, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Here you can see Dragan Andan on the 23rd of July reports to the MUP that these days, a special unit of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina will enter the territory of Brcko, and by its activities it will make it possible for legal organs of authority to function without hindrance. So it is obvious that the problems that you had in Zvornik also occurred in Brcko with the same paramilitary formations, and now the special brigade goes firstly to Brcko at some point around the 23rd or 24th of July, and we know that it arrived to Zvornik on the 29th of July. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that was when some of these groups were arrested. Zuca's group was arrested at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your testimony and the document that was shown to you yesterday, dated the 28th of July, which was forwarded from the Public Security Station Zvornik to the Ministry and security centres in Bijeljina, it wasn't to Sarajevo via Bijeljina, that is to say, in which you report on conflict with Gogic's men and which sounds quite alarming because you are asking urgently for assistance, and you said that two of your colleagues went to Bijeljina asking for help of the special unit which should come to Zvornik. And indeed the special unit arrived on the 27th -- that is to say, the 29th of July; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So when we analyse the genesis of all these reports, we have the first report from the 17th of July [as interpreted] made by Dragomir Andan as a MUP inspector, in which he lists certain problems with which the public security station in Zvornik was facing that we have discussed now. He talks about the presence of the paramilitary units and the problems with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The transcript says the first report from the 17th of July. Can I have some clarification?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 17th of June, I said. It's the first document -- it's the first document that you were -- that I was referring to the witness which you -- which you used in -- in your direct. I believe it's 335, P33 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. That's now exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, P338. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: P338. The transcript came out as 17th July, and I wanted to correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let me return to this. We have the document of the 17th of June in which these problems are noted, the problems that public security station had with paramilitaries. Then we have a document dated the 20th of July in which the same information is repeated but more specifically, and the coming of the special MUP Brigade to Zvornik is requested so that it would resolve this problem with the paramilitaries. Then we have the document dated the 23rd from which we can see that the special brigade already enters Brcko, and we know that the brigade arrived in Zvornik on the 29th of July, and it really did arrest the members of the paramilitary formations. In your opinion, as you are an experienced member of the MUP, when we are talking about such an operation of the MUP directed against a paramilitary formation which has at least 100 members, would that imply that such an operation has to be well planned?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I think that this had to be planned very well, and at that point in time things had to be kept secret. You can see that we did not know that they would be coming, so already on the 28th we could have made things go wrong for them along with Gogic's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So we do agree that this operation had to be carried out in secret, planned in secret, implemented in secret in order to ensure its success, the success of that kind of operation. That is to say, it had to be very serious; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that this absolutely does not resemble the operation that was carried out -- an operation that would have been carried out on an ad hoc basis, perhaps if a minister had a problem with these paramilitaries, rather, this was an operation, an action that was prepared for a certain period of time in order to resolve the problem that the citizens of Zvornik and Brcko encountered, as well as the members of the MUP as well, in relation to the paramilitaries, I mean; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that is the way it was in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps for a bit that was it, but it had to do with the entire territory of the municipality of Zvornik for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After their arrest an investigation was carried out in relation to the activity of these paramilitaries. If you're tired or --

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not. I'm not, I'm not. I have a bit of high blood sugar, and I need water.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At any point if you're unwell -- I can go on.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So after the arrest an investigation was carried out about the misdeeds, if I can put it that way, that were carried out by these paramilitaries. Yesterday 296 from the 65 ter list was shown to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have it called up again on our monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is information provided by the department for combatting crime. Yes. Information, dated the 4th of August, 1992, and it says: "Information on MUP activities on exposing the criminal activity of paramilitary formation Zute Ose, Yellow Wasps in the area of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then it says that in May/June 1992, the security situation in the area of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik was getting complicated because of the activity of the paramilitary formation Zute Osa. There's a mention of Zuco, Repic, and then they were arrested, and what was seized from them, and what the results were of the interviews that were conducted. Also there is a reference to the persons who were detained, if I can put it that way, and so on. And then the very last paragraph on page 3. If we could have that called up, please. It reads as follows: "The information obtained by Serb armed forces, military police, and MUP national security operatives indicate that Dusan Vuckovic also known as Repic committed a massacre-genocide over citizens of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina of Muslim ethnicity. Verification and materialisation of this information was being taken care of -- or, rather, was being taken over by the Serb armed forces military police in cooperation with the MUP operatives." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that due to the nature of the crimes involved - these are crimes that are violations of international humanitarian law and law of war - in the former Yugoslavia it was the military organs that dealt with this and also the military police due to the very nature of these crimes? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as military personnel were concerned, they were tried by military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not only with regard to military personnel, also with regard to these particular forms of crime that were committed in a situation of war.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Panic, do you agree that the release from detention of this person Repic and some other members of the group caused a great deal of protest and fear among MUP members in your area since he had threatened to return to Zvornik or to that area in general? Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And how should I put this? Many were relieved when he was detained in Sabac and Mitrovica and then committed suicide. They were relieved because he would not go back there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure. Yesterday you were shown two documents, P344 and P345. These are documents of the State Security Service, and they were even submitted to the military. They are from as far back as September and October 1992. They speak of these threats, of sorts, that were issued by Repic, saying that he would go back there, that he would return. That is to say that these threats of his and his group's were being taken rather seriously. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, since he was an individual that ran unchecked, and he had Zuco's support and all sorts of things could have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think you said yesterday during your testimony that this special brigade of the MUP, from July 1992, when it first arrived in Zvornik and when they carried out those arrests, that then from time to time they would come to the territory of Zvornik yet again. I assume in order to prevent -- or, rather, intimidate potential paramilitaries from returning to the territory of Zvornik. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, we'd be safer, too, and we'd have more courage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, yesterday during your testimony you said that you were being threatened, too, from Loznica after your conflict with Bogic's men. Did you take these threats seriously?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were assistant commander of the reserve police, if I remember correctly. We discussed that at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was assistant commander for the reserve force before the conflict broke out. After the conflict started, I was assistant commander of the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I meant, before the conflict broke out. Tell me, these members of the police reserve -- how should I put this? They were ordinary people who had done their military service in the then JNA, and by way of a decision of administrative organs, they were transferred to the police reserve. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Upon completing their military service, they would get that kind of assignment. Let them be sent to the reserve of the army or of the police or the civilian protection. So these were reserve wartime assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Objectively speaking, these were persons who had not undergone any kind of police or combat training; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They worked in companies, they worked elsewhere, but they were members of the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, yesterday you talked about the situation in Celopek where Repic committed horrible crimes against persons who were detained there. I think that you then said that the security of that facility was provided by a group of police reservists; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a reserve police station in Celopek, and they at the same time secured the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, these people who provided security, these reserve policemen as we established a moment ago, who, objectively speaking, had not had any kind of special experience, they encountered -- how should I put this? They were up against a criminal. I mean, we can say with good reason that his very personality was a highly disturbed one. I'm referring to Repic. They absolutely did not have -- or, rather, what is your opinion? Did they have any chance of standing up to such a man and his group?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not think that they had a chance of doing that, even if they tried to do something. That's my opinion and I talked to people about this too. If he was alone or, say, with two people, or if something were to be attempted, he would bring more people in. I mean, they were policemen. I mean, we active policemen were not used to that kind of thing either, but reserve policemen in particular, they were not used to shooting at human beings. They were seeking shelter for themselves. They were trying not to get shot themselves. So later on, those who remained were transferred to the prison in Zvornik because the station was closer up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In fact, they were transferred to Novi Izvor in order to protect them as much as possible; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was more protection than in Celopek itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in your view there is no doubt that these reserve policemen were seriously afraid of Repic and that group. They were not in fear only for themselves, but I assume that the members of their families were there too. I mean, they lived in the area. And knowing the structure of his personality, I mean he did not mind who was of which ethnicity. There was his readiness to mistreat and kill anyone for any reason; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. All of these reserve policemen were from there, from Celopek or Trsic, and then people were saying, Well, if he has a knife in his hands and if he put it in his mouth, who would walk up to him? They would just seek shelter trying to hide from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to these facilities if I can put it that way, Novi Izvor and the misdemeanors court. If I'm not mistaken, you said yesterday, and you repeated it today as well, both of these localities were turned into prisons by these paramilitaries and the military police. And at first they provided security there, and it was only later that the police took over the security, if I can put it that way, of these localities, that is to say Novi Izvor and the misdemeanors court; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the military police who provided security at the beginning, and then later, pursuant to a commander's order, the active-duty police took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly the context that we are discussing here, isn't it true that the commander's order to take over the security duties was in fact issued because he wished to try and provide the best possible protection for the detainees? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was precisely that, and pursuant to an agreement with the then provisional government it was decided for the police to take over because these detainees had been maltreated before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Even more so because according to the rules and regulations that are binding for the police and in absence of any order in that sense from the Ministry of the Interior, that meant that you as the police were not duty-bound to secure a prison or a similar institution. There are other organs who take care of that.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In every system, an order to establish a prison should be issued by a court of justice, and based on that, the warden and prison guards are appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. However, in this particular situation that happened in April 1992 in Zvornik, I think that you said in your testimony that initially the period which actually lasted two months, there were totally random arrests made by paramilitary, the police, the Territorial Defence, et cetera. And once these arrests are made, then they would establish a prison and then maltreat the detainees kept there. Is it the correct summary of what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. Both the army and the paramilitaries and whichever unit happened to be there used to arrest people, take them to various facilities, detain them there, because the police at that time never arrested anyone or brought them into custody. That happened only when there was any disturbance of public law and order where they interviewed such people, and then they would be referred to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank my colleague who pointed out a problem in the transcript. 71, 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. We have to clarify this for the benefit of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you -- or, rather, I recapped your testimony in the last two days, and -- and I said that in this particular situation prevailing in April 1992 in Zvornik, I think that in your testimony you said that at the beginning of this period which lasted for two months, arrests were made by paramilitary, the military police, the Territorial Defence, et cetera. Do you remember that, and do you confirm that this was true?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have the problem in the transcript which reads only the police, not the military police, which is a totally erroneous context.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show the witness 65 ter document 180.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document is a direction issued by the Ministry of the Interior, signed by the minister, Mr. Stanisic, and it's dated the 19th of July, 1992. It was sent to all the security services centre. This circular letter was an outcome of the information that appeared, so to say, at the first staff meeting of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, which was held on the 11th of July, 1992, in Belgrade, because that was the only place where all heads of the CSBs could get together. And in this document -- I don't know if you've had an opportunity to see it. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you certain paragraphs, A, G, and E. It was agreed -- A: "Problems related to activities of some paramilitary units -- problems related to activities of some paramilitary units, especially in cases where crimes have been committed ..." Then on page 2, if we can look at that, please. Item G says -- that's D. "Procedures and jurisdiction in the treatment and custody of prisoners, persons evacuated from the combat-operation zones, collection camps into which the army brings Muslim residence without any documents that might state reasons for such action, and then leave such undefined camps to the organs of the interior." And then D says: "Operation of the military judiciary authorities." And lastly the minister sets up the deadline for providing this kind of information. Here it says that the army was taking into detention -- bringing into detention members of the public and population without any documents and then left such camps to the Ministry of the Interior. Wasn't that exactly the situation that you describe as pertaining in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't seen this, but I think that the chief had received such an order for the police to take over the prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, this is not an order. This is a request for providing information, whether there are such cases or not in practice, because that has been highlighted at the 11th of July meeting, that there were incidents in which some kind of undefined camps had been established.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A recommendation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 74, 18, it should say it without any kind of documents stipulating why these people were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you also knew that there were no documents supporting the detention of such individuals were found by the police once they took over [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. No. Only later did the prison warders and guards start keeping records of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you would be so kind to look at document 1D55. This is an order dated the 10th of August, 1992, issued by the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, before we move on to the next document -- before we move on to the next document, I just, in order to keep the record clear, wish to know if you seek to have the last two documents tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, because the witness said he didn't recognise the document. I'm perfectly willing if there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, no, I was just -- I was just asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, I don't have any objection to the admission of those two. I believe they're authentic, and I believe they're relevant and probative. I anticipate that we would be seeking to introduce them later in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we intend to introduce them with the witness, but it is -- it is all the same to us whichever witness is -- is in question. So if there is no objection and it pleases the Court, we will tender this document for an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 296 and 180. Please have them admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D75 and 1D76, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying it resolve an issue. Please bear with me, because there is some issue with the transcript again. [Interpretation] My colleague tells me that on page 74, line 8, I think that the witness said yes to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you, Mr. Panic, that you also knew that no documents had been presented to you relating to the people who were detained and that such documents were not found by the police when they took over the security of these facilities. You said yes, and it says here no. That's why I would like to ask you again what is your answer to this.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yes. We couldn't find any documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at 1D55 now. That's an order issued by the minister of the interior of 10th of August, 1992. It was also distributed to all CSBs. This order was probably prompted by the information that had arrived at the ministry based on the previous document, and here the minister orders the following: That detention and holding measures shall be applied exclusively within the existing regulations, and that he shall hold responsible personally for the lives of people who are being held and detained, and he requests to prevent any kind of abuse of that area. He also requests that the premises where people be held or detained must fulfil basic hygiene and health requirements. And then under 2 he says: "The security of collection centres shall be the direct responsibility of the Serbian Army, and if they do not have enough men for these duties it shall therefore be necessary to engage members of the reserve police for these tasks and place them at the army's disposition." And finally he also says that disciplinary and, if necessary, other measures will be applied. Yesterday you were shown a document in which it was precisely the Territorial Defence who resubordinated a number of reserve policemen. Can you correlate this decision with this order of the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I can't, because the Territorial Defence and the Army of Republika Srpska, who accepted some of our reservists, were part of combat units, because at that time there were no collection centres. They went to Batkovic, and the only prison that remained in Zvornik was Novi Izvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But the Novi Izvor prison in Zvornik was in fact, so to say, the only prison in Zvornik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time that was the only prison that had about 11 or 10 guards, police reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That was, so to say, the basic prison that under normal circumstances every municipality -- or, rather, every court would have. That would be the facility to -- where offenders be kept or people who were in custody; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because that was first a prison before the war, then it was converted into the misdemeanors court, then Novi Izvor and the misdemeanour court were combined and made into one unit because these were adjacent buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, whether in this facility, I'll call it a prison, that at the time there were Serbs who had committed certain crimes -- I even think there was a woman detained there, and there was a Croat as well, which means that their status had nothing to do with their ethnicity but, rather, with the fact that they had committed certain criminal offences. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am, because I heard -- I think that there was a woman called Spomenka Stojkic. She was a Croat and married in Celopek, and I heard that she was in prison and that she had been brought in by the army, that she was guarded by the military police, and later when the prison was taken over by police, she was still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now I'm going to show you yet another document from the minister of the interior in relation to the previous document I showed you, 1D55, dated the 10th August. And now this new document is dated the 17th of April [as interpreted]. 1D005844 is the other document. This was also submitted to all heads of centres of security services. Yet again it is stated: "I hereby repeat the order that all security service centres," et cetera, et cetera, "when dealing with prisoners of war and the civilian population refugees that they act only on the basis of international law of war, international conventions." Then in paragraph 2 having to do with some kind of unofficial prisons and if persons act in contravention of international conventions, the ministry should be informed of violations straight away. And then number 3, as for persons --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can I confirm. In the transcript it indicates the document is dated the 17th of April, but I believe it's 17 August. I just want to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the last paragraph, I can read it out to you: "As for persons violating existing regulations and acting in contravention of our legal provisions and international provisions in this area, regardless of whether these are civilians or members of the MUP or members of the military, immediate action should be taken in order to collect information and documentation in order to file criminal reports to the Office of the Prosecutor in charge." Do you remember this kind of order, a similar order being transmitted to you by your chief?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had not seen the order, but it is only natural that that is the way one should act.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [Previous translation continues] ... admitted into evidence, Your Honours, if there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D77.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just very briefly. Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 332. That is a report on the work of the public security station Novi Zvornik from the 1st of April until the 30th of June, 1992. Now I'm not sure whether it's already been assigned a P number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P346.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I do apologise. So P346, page 2. Page 2, please. I assume that in English it is page 3. Yes. I do apologise. In Serbian it's page 2, and in English it's page 3. Can we see -- I'm sorry. It is page 3, the second page in the document. I do apologise. In English, again it has to be moved one page up again. Sorry. The next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, would you please look at the last paragraph here on the monitor. The basic court in Zvornik, can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a report that was submitted by Vasovic Marinko [as interpreted]. It was shown to you yesterday by my learned friend, and it says here: Since the basic court in Zvornik had not established a guard service for securing the prison, ten employees of the police milicija is in -- without interruption securing the basic prison in Zvornik. In addition to that, there is daily security provided for other facilities, et cetera. What he means here is Novi Izvor; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Novi Izvor is for misdemeanors, but in fact it's one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Seventeen, fifteen, I said Marinko Vasilic, the then chief the public security station in Zvornik. In the transcript it says Vasovic. Do you know whether there were any incidents that took place when members of the paramilitary tried to enter, and sometimes they did succeed in entering facilities that were secured by the police - I'm referring here to the misdemeanors court in Novi Izvor - and that several times, again, the reserve policemen who for the most part provided security for these facilities were mistreated, weapons were pointed at them, knives were put at their throats so that they would unlock the doors in order to allow those individuals to come in and mistreat prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that. I did not see it, but I heard, for example, that a military policeman came in. And on that day or the previous day his brother had got killed and that he entered with a rifle, that he disarmed that guard. He beat him -- or, rather, he beat these Muslims. There were other cases of the kind that I heard of, but since I was not in charge I did not see this personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this gentleman, Mr. Sreto [phoen] Vukovic, who was your colleague, an active-duty policeman, do you know that he was even compelled to engage some locksmiths to change the locks and put bars on the doors in order to make it less possible for persons to barge into prisons during the night and mistreat prisoners? Do you know about that? This has to do with the misdemeanors court and Novi Izvor.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When he was appointed warden -- later on he was appointed warden of the prison. Once he told me that he had to make some reinforcements so that the paramilitaries and the military policemen would not barge in and mistreat people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In view of your numbers, I mean the number of active policemen in the SJB and in view of all the other problems that you had in Zvornik, he could not expect you to give him a group of active policemen to help out with securing these prisons; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you look at our numbers then at the station, at the hotel, perhaps there were one or two extra policemen, but everybody was on patrol or perhaps they went with some units to combat positions. So, no, he could not count on any major help from us, only if we'd happened to be at a particular place. But if we happened to be at a particular place, then -- well, the paramilitary and military policemen, you know, they wouldn't dare. You see, they'd see if we were not in town, then they would -- well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I mean -- right. Basically you were very busy, way too busy, and there were two few of you to carry out that load of work. When you were there and when you could help, and we do have some testimony to that effect, that when Sredo Vukovic would come, then he would manage to -- to deal with these paramilitaries, and he threatened these reserve policemen with some measures to be sent to the front line instead of carrying out these duties, because his order was being violated, that is to say, not to allow anyone to enter the prison premises; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, because after all it is quite different when Sredo's there. After all, he's a trained policeman and an active policeman, rather than someone who just came from a factory and was dressed in a uniform and was given a rifle and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [Previous translation continues] ... another, I believe, ten minutes for tomorrow just to cover the issues that Mr. Hannis covered this morning, and I believe I will be -- there is no point in starting because it's completely new issue now, and I would finish tomorrow, I believe, in 15 minutes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 13th day of November, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
